terms.grammar: imperative of faciō, with an accusative and infinitive
evidence: Cic. Tusc. 1.82: fac … animōs nōn remanēre post mortem
Cic. Fam. 7.23.1: fac, quaesō, quī ego sum esse tē
terms.comment: Lewis & Short: fac, used hypothetically, “suppose, assume”. Not fac ut, make sure that (see sure).

terms.grammar: verb, third conjugation, with an accusative and infinitive: finge, fingāmus
evidence: Cic. Ac. 2.117: finge aliquem nunc fierī sapientem, nōndum esse
Quint. 1.1.24: fingāmus igitur Alexandrum darī nōbīs

terms.grammar: with the subjunctive of a supposed case
evidence: Ter. Eun. 368: Quid sī nunc tūte fortūnātus fīās?

phrases.latin: sed fac, ut istī volunt, animōs nōn remanēre post mortem
phrases.english: but suppose, as those people would have it, that souls do not survive death

phrases.latin: fingāmus igitur Alexandrum darī nōbīs impositum gremiō, dignum tantā cūrā īnfantem (quamquam suus cuique dignus est)
phrases.english: so let us imagine that an Alexander is given to us and laid in our lap, a baby worthy of so much care (though everyone’s own child is worthy of it)

phrases.latin: Quid sī nunc tūte fortūnātus fīās?
phrases.english: What if you were the lucky one now?

sources: Lewis & Short: facio · Lewis & Short: fingo · Lewis & Short: si
Cicero (Tusc. 1.82, Fam. 7.23.1, Ac. 2.117), Quintilian (1.1.24) and Terence (Eun. 368) checked against the Perseus Latin texts (9 November 2026).
